# Probability, and how a machine learns it {#sec-ch02}

::: {.epigraph by="Joseph Butler, The Analogy of Religion, 1736"}
But to us, probability is the very guide of life.
:::

"Probability? Coins and dice. I did it at school, and I don't need it to build AI."

That thought is the most expensive mistake in this field.

The last chapter's machine was useless because we asked it for *yes* or *no*. The fix was to ask for a *chance*. This chapter makes sure you can read a chance without being fooled, including the one trap that catches doctors, judges and security teams. Then it shows how a machine learns chances from examples. No difficult maths: just a few ideas you'll use for the rest of your career.

::: {.goals}
- Say what "a 70% chance" means in a way you could check.
- Notice the base-rate trap before it costs you, and update a probability by multiplying odds.
- Read precision and recall, and explain why accuracy can lie.
- Explain how a model adds up evidence into a probability, how it's scored, and how it learns by rolling downhill.
- Recognise overfitting and leakage, the two ways a model fools you during training.
:::

## What "70%" means

Your weather app says 70% chance of rain. It stays dry. Was the forecast wrong?

One day can't tell you. The forecaster's *record* can. Collect every day they said "70%". If it rained on about 70 of every 100 of those days, they're doing their job, and today was one of the 30.

::: {.keyidea}
A **probability** is a claim about how often something happens among cases like this one.
:::

This definition is useful because you can *check* it. A model that calls an alert "70% likely to be an attack" is making the weather app's promise, and can be checked the same way.

## The two most important words: "among what?"

At Kestrel, about {{< num ch02 base pct1 >}} of all alerts are real attacks. That's the chance of an attack **among all alerts**. Among alerts with a bad threat score (0.7 or more), it's {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}}. Same question; the answer depends on *which group* you ask about.

This is written P(attack | bad score), read "the chance of an attack *given* a bad score". Now the confusing part: it is not the same as P(bad score | attack). Only {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} of attacks come with a bad score, but that doesn't make a bad-score alert {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} likely to be an attack. "How often do attacks look like this?" and "how often is something that looks like this an attack?" are different questions. In courts, mixing them up is called the *prosecutor's fallacy*, and it has put innocent people in prison.

## The trap

Try this puzzle before reading on. A new detector catches 99% of real attacks. It also raises a false alarm on 5% of normal activity. Real attacks are rare: one event in every thousand. The detector just fired. What's the chance you're looking at a real attack?

Most people say about 95%. The real answer is about **2%**.

In a famous 1978 study, doctors and students at Harvard Medical School got the same puzzle about a medical test, and the most common answer was 95% [@casscells1978]. The way out is to count, not to use a formula.

![The same puzzle, counted out. Of 100,000 events, 100 are attacks and the detector catches 99 of them. But 5% of the 99,900 normal events also set it off: 4,995 false alarms. When the alarm sounds, you're holding one of 5,094 alerts, and only 99 of them are real.](/figures/ch02/base-rate-tree.pdf){#fig-base-rate-tree}

The 5% false-alarm rate sounds small, but it's 5% of a *huge* number. The 99% hit rate sounds large, but it's 99% of a *tiny* one (@fig-base-rate-tree). People who think in counts like these get such puzzles right far more often [@gigerenzer1995]. Whenever a probability surprises you, turn it into counts.

The chance of something before you see any evidence, here 1 in 1,000, is called the **base rate**. Ignoring it is the base-rate fallacy. It's why a "95% accurate" fraud model can still drown a bank in false alarms.

::: {.keyidea}
Rare things stay rare even after the alarm goes off.
:::

## Bayes' rule, made simple

How *should* a new clue change your mind? Use **odds**, "for" against "against": 20% is odds of 20 to 80, or 0.25. Each clue has a strength: how much more common it is among attacks than among harmless alerts. That's its **likelihood ratio**. A threat score of 0.7 or more shows up in {{< num ch02 ioc_attack_share pct >}} of attacks and {{< num ch02 ioc_benign_share pct1 >}} of harmless alerts. So its likelihood ratio is about {{< num ch02 lr_ioc f1 >}}.

Then Bayes' rule, the famous one, fits on one line:

::: {.keyidea}
New odds = old odds × likelihood ratio.
:::

![Starting from the base rate and multiplying the odds by each clue's likelihood ratio. Three ordinary clues take an alert from "probably nothing" to "probably an attack".](/figures/ch02/odds-update.pdf){#fig-odds-update}

An ordinary alert starts at {{< num ch02 base pct >}}. A bad threat-intel score takes it to {{< num ch02 p1 pct >}}. Add "outside business hours" and it's {{< num ch02 p2 pct >}}; add "sign-in from a new country" and it's {{< num ch02 p3 pct >}} (@fig-odds-update).

One warning: multiplying assumes each clue tells you something *new*. Real clues overlap (attackers using known-bad servers also tend to work at night). Among alerts with both clues, {{< num ch02 real12 pct >}} are real, not the {{< num ch02 p2 pct >}} the multiplication predicted. That's why, in practice, we let a model learn how much each clue is worth.

## Why accuracy lies

How do you score a yes-or-no rule? Take *flag every alert with a threat score of 0.5 or more*, and sort all alerts into four boxes.

![Every one of the 20,000 alerts, sorted by what the rule said and what really happened. Precision and recall each ignore one of the two columns, which makes them fair judges of rare events.](/figures/ch02/confusion.pdf){#fig-confusion}

**Precision** answers: *when the rule raises an alert, how often is it real?* Here it's {{< num ch02 precision pct >}}. **Recall** answers: *of all the real attacks, how many did the rule catch?* Here it's {{< num ch02 recall pct >}}. And **accuracy** is the share of all alerts put in the right box (@fig-confusion). It comes out at {{< num ch02 accuracy pct >}}. That sounds good, until you notice that a rule that *never raises any alert at all* scores {{< num ch02 always_benign_acc pct >}}. When one outcome is rare, accuracy mostly measures how common the other one is.

## A model that adds up evidence

Now a machine that learns these probabilities. Bayes multiplied odds; adding is easier. Take the logarithm of the odds, the **log-odds**, and every multiplication becomes an addition. The machine is then simple: start from a base number, add a **weight** for each clue, and turn the total into a probability with an S-shaped curve.

![The S-curve (the logistic, or sigmoid, function) turns total evidence into a probability. Every step to the right multiplies the odds by the same amount, which is why the curve flattens out: once you're very sure, more evidence changes the probability only a little.](/figures/ch03/sigmoid.pdf){#fig-sigmoid}

That's **logistic regression** (@fig-sigmoid), behind credit scores and medical risk scores for decades. It's Bayes' rule on the log-odds scale with one improvement: it learns all the weights *together*, so overlapping clues don't get counted twice. The weights are the knobs. To set them, we need to define "good".

## Scoring a probability

Counting mistakes no longer works: the model says 0.07 or 0.63, not yes or no. How would you want a forecaster judged? Say 90% and be right: lose almost nothing. Say 1% and be wrong: lose a lot, for being confidently wrong. That score is **log loss**, a measure of surprise: the penalty is minus the logarithm of the probability you gave to what actually happened.

![Log loss for a single alert. If it really was an attack (red, solid curve), the penalty is small when the model gave "attack" a high probability. It grows very fast as that probability gets close to zero. Harmless alerts (blue, dashed curve) work the same way from the other side.](/figures/ch03/logloss.pdf){#fig-logloss}

Saying 90% and being right costs about {{< num ch03 loss_if_right_09 f1 >}}. Saying 1% and being wrong costs about {{< num ch03 loss_if_certain_wrong f1 >}}, nearly fifty times more (@fig-logloss).

Log loss has a deeper property, and the whole book leans on it. It's a **proper scoring rule**: the only way to get the best score on average is to report what you actually believe. Say 99% when you believe 80%, and over many cases you lose. So models trained on log loss tend to come out close to honest, or *calibrated*.

::: {.keyidea}
Log loss rewards calibrated probabilities and punishes confident mistakes.
:::

## Rolling downhill

Picture log loss as hilly ground: every combination of weights is a place, and the height is the loss. Learning means finding the lowest point. You don't need to search everywhere. Stand on the hill in thick fog, feel which way the ground slopes, step downhill, repeat. That's **gradient descent**. The **gradient** is the slope; the size of each step is the **learning rate**. Too small and you barely move; too big and you step right over the valley.

![The loss surface for a tiny model with just two knobs. The contours are like a map's height lines. Gradient descent starts from a deliberately bad guess and follows the slope down to the valley floor.](/figures/ch03/descent-2d.pdf){#fig-descent-2d}

Run that loop four hundred times on Kestrel's alerts, then test on alerts held back from training (the only fair test). The result comes within {{< num ch03 gap_pct pct >}} of the best score *any* model could reach on this data; because the data is synthetic, we know the true probabilities and can check.

That loop, *predict, measure the surprise, step downhill*, is the centre of machine learning. Training an LLM is the same loop with a vastly bigger model, more data and smarter steps.

::: {.keyidea}
All of machine learning is one loop: predict, measure the surprise, step downhill.
:::

## Two ways a model fools you

**Overfitting** is memorising instead of learning. A flexible enough model can fit every small detail of the training data, including the noise. Its training loss keeps falling while it gets *worse* at anything new.

![A decision tree allowed only a few questions learns general patterns. Allowed dozens, it memorises individual training alerts: its loss on them approaches zero while its loss on new alerts climbs.](/figures/ch03/overfit.pdf){#fig-overfit}

A decision tree asks a chain of yes-or-no questions. Allowed {{< num ch03 tree_best_depth int >}} levels, it does best on new alerts. Allowed twenty, it nearly memorises its training alerts (loss {{< num ch03 tree_deep_train f3 >}}) and does badly on new ones ({{< num ch03 tree_deep_test f2 >}}) (@fig-overfit). You only see this by testing on data the model never trained on.

**Leakage** is harder to spot and more dangerous. It's when a clue secretly contains the answer.

::: {.breaks}
Suppose the alert database has a field of analyst notes. Train with it and results look amazing, because notes like "confirmed phishing" are written *after* someone decided. When the model has to decide, that field is empty. Ask this about every clue: *would I actually have this value at the moment of the decision?* And remember that probabilities are always "among cases like this". If attackers start a campaign, the base rate jumps. Then every probability computed from last month is suddenly too low.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Precision and recall pull in opposite directions. Lower the rule's threshold from 0.5 to 0.3. Which one goes up, and which goes down? If the team can only check 300 alerts a day, which should they care about more?

(Recall goes up and precision goes down: you catch more attacks and raise more false alarms. With a fixed daily limit, precision decides how many real attacks are among those 300 alerts. Chapter 4 puts both into a single cost.)
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. A spam filter catches 98% of spam and wrongly flags 1% of real email. If 20% of incoming email is spam, what fraction of flagged emails are real? Now try a mailbox where only 1% is spam. Use counts, as in @fig-base-rate-tree.
2. Name a clue in your own work that would be *leakage*: available when you train, but not when you decide.
:::
